planting.note: Direct sow in early spring in full to part sun in lean, sandy, well-drained soil; Simpson's rosinweed is a peninsular Florida endemic of sandhills, scrub margins, and open pine flatwoods and resents heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, sharply drained soil in full to part sun; Simpson's rosinweed is a Florida endemic sometimes classified as a variety of starry rosinweed, but it stands apart with a taller, more branched habit and a longer summer-into-fall bloom season of bright yellow daisy flowers. Like other members of the genus it produces resinous sap in its stems, and the abundant blooms are a magnet for native bees, butterflies, and beneficial wasps throughout the growing season. It thrives on neglect in hot, sandy sites where richer garden soil would cause it to flop, and mature plants develop a deep taproot that shrugs off Florida's seasonal drought.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into thin, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; stone mountain mint occurs naturally on granite and mafic rock outcrops and dry rocky woodlands across the southern Appalachian foothills and resents rich, moisture-retentive garden beds.

directions: Grow in shallow, mineral, sharply drained soil over rock in full sun to light shade, mimicking the granite outcrops and mafic glades of Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, and Tennessee where this rare mountain mint survives in scattered small populations. The purple-spotted summer flower clusters, like those of its more common relatives, are exceptionally attractive to a wide range of specialist and generalist native bees. Because natural populations are sparse and vulnerable, gardeners in its native range who succeed with it are contributing a meaningful conservation planting rather than simply another mint for the border. Avoid fertile, water-retentive soils, which favor competitors it cannot tolerate in the wild.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
